newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany rejects Iranian charge of interference.
newsitem.headline: Germany rejects Iranian charge of interference.

text.p: Germany on Thursday rejected an Iranian accusation that it was interfering in Tehran's internal affairs by asking for information about an Iranian journalist detained for allegedy trying to leave the country illegally.

"Encouraging and observing elementary human rights is a legitimate concern of the international community and an important touchstone for relations with any country," a German Foreign Ministry spokesman said.

State Tehran Radio earlier on Thursday quoted an Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman as saying the arrest and trial of Faraj Sarkuhi was an internal affair and any foreign interference was "unacceptable".
Bonn has asked Tehran to explain reports that Sarkuhi had not only been detained and tortured for 47 days last year when he was supposedly in Germany, but had now been arrested again.
Iran has told Bonn he was arrested in southwest Iran on February 2 while trying to leave the country illegally.
The German Foreign Ministry has said documents provided by Iran to prove Sarkuhi visited Germany late last year -- when he says he was being tortured in detention -- were probably false.

Sarkuhi said in a letter, published recently in several German newspapers, he had been held by the Iranian secret service and tortured into confessing in a taped interview that he had spied for Germany.
He said in the letter, which Bonn believes is genuine, he feared Tehran planned to use the confession in its row with Germany over a Berlin murder case.
Prosecutors have accused Iran of ordering the 1992 killings of three dissidents and their translator in a Berlin restaurant. The verdict in the case is expected within the next few months.
A German parliamentarian echoed Sarkuhi's fears, saying he was concerned Iran may try to use the him as a bargaining chip in the Berlin case.
An Iranian and four Lebanese are being tried for the gangland-style killings in a Berlin restaurant. Iran denies any involvement.
Rudolf Bindig, human rights spokesman for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), told German Radio he was unaware of any legitimate reason Tehran had for arresting Sarkuhi.

"I don't know that Mr Sarkuhi committed any crimes, any crimes at least that would be recognised internationally as crimes," Bindig said. "From the regime's perspective, it may certainly be a crime' if one has contacts to foreigners."

Bindig said a second possible explanation for Sarkuhi's could be to start a domestic campaign against Germany and a third reason could be that Iran wanted to discredit Sarkuhi and other intellectuals.

Sarkuhi, the editor of the monthly Adineh (Friday) magazine, was one of six Iranian writers held briefly after security agents burst into a dinner function at the Tehran home of the German cultural attache Jens Gust in July. Iran expressed regret over the incident after Bonn protested the action.
